anchors.fact: Siegal was one of the few friends Petraske made at Stuyvesant, his high school (*Proper*, p. 86). Petraske had talked about the bar for a few months before he told Siegal the plumber was coming and he had no money. Siegal's own gloss: it wasn't a request to invest; it was "I ran out of money" (*A Proper Drink*, p. 88, Siegal's account). Undated: the late 1990s, before the opening on New Year's Eve 1999.
anchors.meaning: He heard "help" in a sentence about plumbing. Nobody asked.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: hears the ask nobody made

anchors.fact: For months, Siegal handed over all the cash he made at the restaurant where he worked (p. 88). Proper calls it lending seed money (p. 96). A couple of other school friends took on credit-card debt too (p. 88).
anchors.meaning: Slow, dull, costly, and for one friend. Not a rescue, not a speech.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: nobody they love has to ask properly

anchors.fact: Early 2002: Petraske went to London for six months and left Milk & Honey in the hands of Siegal and Joseph Schwartz (p. 95).
anchors.meaning: He minded the thing his friend loved while his friend was away (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: there for as long as it takes

anchors.fact: When the *New York Times* wrote the bar up in May 2000 (Chaplin, 7 May 2000; Oxford MILK & HONEY bibliography, pdf 1304), Petraske was livid and thought it made him look bad. Siegal didn't agree: "I bought thirty copies" (p. 93).
anchors.meaning: I like to think that was the sentence he never said out loud (our reading, signposted: the page gives no reason, and doesn't say what he did with them).

anchors.fact: The Gold Rush: Siegal asked Petraske for "one of those whiskey sours" with the honey syrup instead of the sugar: "It was as simple as that" (p. 96). He had the idea sitting at the bar after a long shift; his usual was a Bourbon Sour "on the rocks, without egg or garnish", as on many nights before (*PUNCH* 2021).
anchors.meaning: A blunt standing order, one change, and it came out rich (p. 96's own judgement, in our words).
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof: blunt order, full-size feeling

anchors.fact: Siegal named it: "He christened it the Gold Rush." He likes names that bring a feeling, a thought or a chuckle, with no hidden meaning (*PUNCH* 2021).
anchors.meaning: Even his names don't make speeches.
anchors.speaksTo: voice: short, dry, allowed to be funny

anchors.fact: Proper: Siegal is "not a drink creator", and his role was "largely unheralded" (p. 96). The Gold Rush was an early hit, soon made at other bars (p. 96); Oxford lists it among Milk & Honey's modern classics (pdf 1304). Around 2012 he found it chalked up at Union Square Cafe under "Classic Cocktails", last after the Old-Fashioned, Manhattan, Sazerac and Martini; he was "a little bit shocked, a little bit suspicious, and a little bit giddy" (*PUNCH* 2021).
anchors.meaning: A renowned modern classic from a man nobody credits. Worth having.
anchors.speaksTo: let the drink sound worth having; the unseen deed

anchors.fact: The honey syrup: Petraske started making it (Siegal, p. 96) for an old drink, the Honeysuckle; Toby Maloney had a hand in the 3:1 house syrup (*PUNCH* 2021). Our syrup: 3:1 by volume (*Codex* p. 45), with clover, the commonest grocery honey (*Codex* p. 45), "spiced" in the Matrix's word (pdf 148).
anchors.meaning: His friend's work, in Siegal's telling, in the one change he asked for.

anchors.fact: Bourbon: Proper recommends Elijah Craig (p. 96, "single batch"); *PUNCH* has Knob Creek for the first and Elijah Craig 12-year-old as the house bourbon after. That 12-year-old was sold as Elijah Craig Small Batch until its age statement came off in January 2016 (*The Spirits Business*, 2016; our inference that it's the same bottle). The *Codex*'s own Whiskey Sour uses Elijah Craig Small Batch (p. 130). Arnold's own Gold Rush (LI p. 133) uses a 47% bourbon, no bottle named.
anchors.meaning: The bottle a guest can buy under the name the house poured. Never "the same whiskey".

anchors.fact: Proper prints a 30-second shake (p. 96). Arnold: 8 to 12 seconds gives about the same drink; past 12 "almost nothing additional happens" (LI pp. 97–98; chilling and dilution). Reading y4: "After about twelve seconds, the drink barely changes." Closing line: "The cold's done by twelve", never "needs twelve".
anchors.meaning: The seconds past the cold are hands busy, back to the room.
anchors.speaksTo: position: say it while your hands are busy

anchors.fact: Proper prints ¾ oz honey syrup (p. 96, page image). Ours is ½ oz (15 ml against 22.5), a third less: the printed measure reads OUT on Arnold's sugar range for sours (12.19 vs 8.9 g/100 ml, `balance.py`; LI pp. 129–130), and ½ oz lands (8.73). Arnold's own Gold Rush (LI p. 133) uses ¾ oz of his thinner, by-weight honey syrup.
anchors.meaning: "So the bourbon gets a word in": our choice, stated as ours. Never "his recipe".
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; the position (a word in)

anchors.fact: "The thirty seconds and the thirty copies" (coincidence).
anchors.meaning: Owned in one plain clause if both appear; otherwise "half a minute" (Tomás).

cocktail.closingLine: Thirty seconds of shaking. The cold's done by twelve. Say it in the other eighteen.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass, one large plain cube (the biggest cube your freezer makes; not clear, not cut)
method: Make the honey syrup: three spoons of light runny honey and one of water in a jar, lid on, shaken until it's smooth.
Put one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Pour the bourbon, lemon and honey syrup into a shaker and fill it three-quarters with ice.
Close it and shake hard for thirty seconds.
Strain it over the cube. Nothing on top.
cocktail.name: Any Day

recipe.note: Elijah Craig Small Batch recommended, or any straight bourbon between 40% and 50%
three parts light runny honey (wildflower, or a light clover) to one part water, shaken in a closed jar until smooth

cocktail.tagline: Nobody you love ever has to ask you. They only have to mention it.

reading.epigraph: Ordered after a long shift: the usual, with honey instead of sugar. Now it's a classic.
whoYouAre: Someone you love mentions that the car's making that noise again. That's all. They'd never ask, and they don't need to: you heard it, because it's exactly how you'd have said it. By Saturday you're flat on your back underneath it, and neither of you makes a thing of it. A mention is enough. What comes back isn't a card or a speech. It's the thing done, for as long as it takes.

The sentence you've never quite managed is the other one, the one that says why. The feeling's there, full size. Said out loud, it sounds like someone else's words, so it stays put, and you tell yourself they know. Mostly they do. But now and then, on a long drive home, you think about the day it'll be too late to check. Here's what your way gives the people you love: they never have to find the words to ask, and they never owe you a thank-you. They always know where they can lean. That's worth more than any speech.
yours: In the late 1990s, Sasha Petraske was turning a tiny former tailor's shop in New York into a bar, and he ran out of money. He told T. J. Siegal, one of the few friends he'd made at school, that the plumber was coming and he didn't have any money. Siegal was clear, years later: it wasn't a request to invest. It was a friend saying he'd run out.

So for months, Siegal handed over all the cash he made at the restaurant where he worked. When the *New York Times* wrote the bar up, Petraske was furious; he thought it made him look bad. Siegal's answer, as he tells it, is four words: "I bought thirty copies." Maybe it was just good for business. I like to think it was the closest he came to saying he was proud of his friend.

You'd have heard it too. Not a money problem: help, from someone who hadn't asked. And you'd have answered in the same language: no speech, just months of turning up. And when you're proud of someone, you'd rather buy thirty copies than say so.

Sitting at the bar one night after a long shift, Siegal asked for his usual bourbon sour, with the honey syrup Petraske had started making instead of the sugar. "It was as simple as that," he said. He named it the Gold Rush, and years later found it chalked up under classic cocktails, last on a list that began with the Old-Fashioned and the Manhattan. It made him "a little bit giddy". The cocktail I've made for you starts from his order, as the recipe prints it: bourbon, lemon and honey syrup, shaken hard, over one large cube of ice, no egg, nothing on top. I've used a third less honey syrup than the printed recipe, so the bourbon gets a word in, the way I'd like you to. It's shaken for thirty seconds, as the recipe says. Thirty again: a coincidence, nothing more. After about twelve seconds, the drink barely changes.

Forget the speech. Nobody who loves you is waiting for one. You need one line, said while you're busy with something else. Under the car. Halfway through the job. On the drive home, eyes on the road. "I'd do this for you any day" is plenty. They've always known where they can lean. Now they'll know why.
